The best laptop for AI depends on how much GPU memory it has, because memory decides which AI models you can run. The one rule: memory decides what you can run

Use our VRAM calculator and see how much VRAM you need for an LLM.

Laptop GPU options for AI (2026)

Important: laptop GPUs share names with desktop cards but are much slower and lower-powered. A laptop RTX 5090 has 24 GB, not the desktop's 32 GB. See RTX 5090 for AI.

Best laptops for AI by use case

1. Best for machine learning and deep learning (CUDA)

Pick: a 16–18-inch gaming or workstation laptop with an RTX 5090 laptop GPU (24 GB) and 64 GB system RAM.

Examples include the ASUS ROG Strix Scar 16/18, Lenovo Legion 9i/Pro 7i, MSI Raider/Titan and Razer Blade 16/18 with RTX 5090. Workstation alternatives such as the Dell Pro Max 16/18 Plus with an RTX PRO 5000 (24 GB) offer certified drivers at a much higher price.

  • Runs PyTorch, CUDA, TensorRT and almost all research code.
  • Fine-tunes 7–8B models with QLoRA; see What is LoRA?
  • Generates images quickly; see best GPU for Stable Diffusion.

2. Best for running large LLMs locally

Pick: MacBook Pro with M5 Max and 64–128 GB unified memory.

  • 128 GB runs 70B dense models and ~120B MoE models such as gpt-oss-120b.
  • Up to ~614 GB/s bandwidth gives good generation speed.
  • Silent operation and all-day battery for lighter tasks.
  • Use LM Studio (MLX) or Ollama; see best Mac for local LLMs.

3. Best value for large models on Windows or Linux

Pick: a laptop with AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 and 128 GB (for example HP ZBook Ultra G1a or ASUS ROG Flow Z13).

  • Up to 96 GB of memory can be assigned to the GPU (more on Linux).
  • Runs 70B models and ~100B MoE models, more slowly than an M5 Max.
  • See Ryzen AI Max+ 395 for local LLMs and ROCm vs CUDA.

4. Best for students learning AI and data science

Pick: an RTX 5070 Ti or RTX 5080 laptop (12–16 GB) with 32 GB RAM, or a MacBook Pro/Air with 24–32 GB if you mostly use Python, notebooks and cloud GPUs.

  • Most coursework runs on small models or cloud notebooks.
  • CUDA matters if your course uses GPU training locally.
  • Budget for cloud GPUs for large jobs: our GPU price tracker lists RTX 4090s from about $0.26/hour and H100s from about $1.80/hour.

5. Best lightweight AI laptop

Pick: MacBook Air or MacBook Pro (M6 or M5 Pro) with 24–32 GB, or a Copilot+ PC with 32 GB.

  • Runs 8–14B models smoothly for writing, coding help and chat.
  • Excellent battery life.

6. Best budget AI laptop

Pick: an RTX 5060 laptop (8 GB) with 16–32 GB RAM.

  • Good for learning, small models and SD 1.5 image generation.
  • Expect to rely on the cloud for anything large.

Do NPUs matter for AI?

Neural processing units (NPUs) in Intel Core Ultra, AMD Ryzen AI and Snapdragon chips (typically 40–50+ TOPS) power Windows features like Copilot+ effects, live captions and background blur efficiently. For running LLMs, image generation or training, the GPU and its memory matter far more: a laptop RTX 5090 offers well over 1,000 AI TOPS. See NPU vs GPU vs TPU, What is an AI PC? and TOPS vs TFLOPS.

Laptop vs desktop vs cloud

Many people combine a capable laptop with cloud GPUs. See rent vs buy a GPU and the AI workstation build guide.

Buying checklist

1. GPU memory first: 16 GB VRAM minimum for serious CUDA work; 64 GB+ unified memory for large LLMs. 2. Check GPU power (TGP): the same GPU can run at very different wattages in different laptops; higher TGP means faster. 3. System RAM: 32 GB minimum, 64 GB for ML work on Windows/Linux. 4. Storage: 1–2 TB NVMe; models are large (a 70B model is around 40 GB at 4-bit). 5. Cooling: thick laptops sustain performance better. 6. Operating system: Linux or WSL2 for CUDA development; macOS for MLX; check ROCm support for AMD. 7. Upgradeability: RAM is soldered on most Macs and unified-memory laptops; buy enough upfront. 8. Battery and weight: high-end GPU laptops often last only a few hours under load.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best laptop for running LLMs locally?

A MacBook Pro with M5 Max and 128 GB unified memory runs the largest models; an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 laptop with 128 GB is a cheaper Windows/Linux alternative. For CUDA, an RTX 5090 laptop with 24 GB VRAM is fastest for models up to about 32B.

Is a MacBook good for AI?

Yes for running models and general AI development, thanks to large unified memory and efficiency. It lacks CUDA, so some training libraries and research code don't run natively.

How much RAM do I need for AI on a laptop?

32 GB system RAM for most AI work with a discrete GPU; 64–128 GB of unified memory if you want to run large models on a Mac or Strix Halo laptop.

Is an RTX 4090 laptop still good for AI?

Yes. The RTX 4090 laptop has 16 GB VRAM and remains capable, especially used.

Do I need a powerful laptop to learn machine learning?

No. Free and cheap cloud notebooks handle most learning. A mid-range laptop plus cloud GPUs is often the most economical setup.

The best Mac for local LLMs is the one with the most unified memory and memory bandwidth you can afford. In 2026, the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra (up to 512 GB and 1.2 TB/s) can run models with hundreds of billions of parameters; the Mac Studio or MacBook Pro with M5 Max (up to 128 GB, up to 614 GB/s) is the sweet spot for 70B dense and ~120B mixture-of-experts models; the M5 Pro Mac mini (up to 64 GB, 307 GB/s, from $1,699) is the best value for 30B-class models; and the M6 Mac mini (16–32 GB, from $899) handles 8–14B models. Why Macs are good for local LLMs

  • Unified memory: the GPU can use most of the system memory, so a 128 GB Mac can load models no consumer NVIDIA card can hold (the RTX 5090 has 32 GB).
  • High bandwidth: Max and Ultra chips have hundreds of GB/s to over 1 TB/s.
  • Efficiency: quiet, low power, no huge PSU or cooling.
  • Great software: MLX, LM Studio, Ollama and llama.cpp all support Apple Silicon well.

Downsides: no CUDA, slower prompt processing than high-end NVIDIA GPUs (improved substantially by the Neural Accelerators in M5-generation GPU cores), expensive memory upgrades, and no upgrades after purchase.

The current Mac lineup for AI (late 2026)

Bandwidth is the speed limit

When generating text, the computer reads the model's active weights for every token. A rough upper limit is:

max tokens/second ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ model size in memory

Real speeds are typically 60–80% of these ceilings. Mixture-of-experts models are much faster than their total size suggests because only active parameters are read per token. See GPU memory bandwidth and mixture of experts.

Reported benchmarks

A widely used llama.cpp benchmark (Llama 2 7B, Q4_0) reported roughly 36 tok/s on M6, 68 on M5 Pro, 120 on M5 Max and 179 on M5 Ultra in one October 2026 roundup, and about 88 tok/s for gpt-oss-120b on an M5 Max at short context. Treat community figures as approximate; results vary with software version, context length and GPU core count.

  • For the M5 Max, the 40-core GPU version has 33% more bandwidth than the 32-core.

Apple says a cluster of four Mac Studios can speed up inference. Tools like Exo and MLX distributed split models across Macs connected by Thunderbolt 5. It is a niche but growing way to run the very largest models at home.

Frequently asked questions

How much RAM does a Mac need for local LLMs?

32 GB is the practical minimum for useful models; 64 GB runs 30B-class models comfortably; 128 GB or more is needed for 70B dense and 100B+ MoE models.

Yes. The M5 Pro Mac mini with 64 GB is one of the best-value local AI computers; the M6 Mac mini suits smaller models.

Is Mac Studio better than an RTX 5090 for AI?

For large models, yes, because it has far more memory. For models that fit in 32 GB, the RTX 5090 is faster and supports CUDA.

Can a Mac fine-tune LLMs?

Yes, with MLX (LoRA and QLoRA) for small and medium models, though NVIDIA GPUs remain faster for training. See What is LoRA?

Should I buy the M5 Ultra with 512 GB?

Only if you need to run the largest open models locally; for most people, 128 GB covers excellent models at far lower cost.

content:
Short answer

Learning how to train an LLM from scratch comes down to nine stages: define the goal and budget, collect and clean text data, train a tokenizer, choose a model size, implement a transformer, pretrain it on next-token prediction, post-train it to follow instructions, evaluate it, and deploy it. Compute is the main cost: training needs roughly 6 × parameters × training tokens floating-point operations. A small 124M-parameter GPT-2-style model can be trained in hours for tens of dollars, a 1B model on 20B tokens takes roughly 80–100 H100 GPU-hours (a few hundred dollars), while a 7B model on 1 trillion tokens needs around 30,000 H100-hours (over $100,000). For most real products, fine-tuning an existing open model is cheaper and better; training from scratch is ideal for learning, research and specialised domains.

Should you train from scratch?

If your goal is a production assistant, start with fine-tuning. If your goal is to understand or innovate, training from scratch is invaluable.

The nine stages

Step 1: Define the goal and budget

Decide:

  • Purpose: learning, research, a domain model, a small on-device model?
  • Compute budget: GPU-hours and dollars. Use our training cost calculator and LLM training cost guide.
  • Constraints: context length, languages, target hardware for inference.

Step 2: Collect and prepare data

Data quality matters more than almost anything else.

Processing pipeline:

1. Extract text from HTML/PDF. 2. Language identification. 3. Quality filtering (heuristics and classifiers, such as FineWeb-Edu's educational-quality classifier). 4. Deduplication (exact and fuzzy, e.g. MinHash). 5. Remove personal data and toxic content. 6. Decontaminate: remove benchmark test sets from training data. 7. Mix sources in chosen proportions. 8. Tokenize and shard into binary files for fast loading.

Step 3: Train a tokenizer

Most LLMs use byte-pair encoding (BPE) or similar subword methods. Typical vocabulary sizes range from 32,000 to over 200,000 tokens. Larger vocabularies compress text better (fewer tokens per word, especially for multilingual text) but add embedding parameters.

from tokenizers import Tokenizer, models, trainers, pre_tokenizers

tok = Tokenizer(models.BPE())
tok.pre_tokenizer = pre_tokenizers.ByteLevel()
trainer = trainers.BpeTrainer(vocab_size=32000, special_tokens=["<|endoftext|>"])
tok.train(["data.txt"], trainer)
tok.save("tokenizer.json")

Or reuse an existing tokenizer (GPT-2's via tiktoken, or an open model's). See What are tokens in AI?

Step 4: Choose model size with scaling laws

DeepMind's Chinchilla study (2022) found compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter. Modern models often train far longer than that (for example, Meta trained Llama 3 8B on about 15 trillion tokens, nearly 2,000 tokens per parameter) because smaller, over-trained models are cheaper to run. See scaling laws explained.

Step 5: Estimate compute, time and cost

Training FLOPs ≈ 6 × N × D, where N is parameters and D is training tokens.

Assume an H100 at 989 TFLOPS dense BF16 running at 40% utilisation (MFU) ≈ 4 × 1014 useful FLOP/s, and the November 2026 median H100 rental price of $3.92/hour from our GPU price tracker.

Real costs are higher: experiments, failed runs, evaluation and data processing add a lot. For reference, Meta reported about 1.46 million H100 GPU-hours to train Llama 3.1 8B. Andrej Karpathy's llm.c project reproduced GPT-2 (124M) in about 90 minutes on one 8×A100 node for roughly $20 in 2024. See MFU explained.

Step 6: Choose the architecture

Step 7: Write and test the training loop

A minimal PyTorch training step:

import torch
model = GPT(config).cuda()
model = torch.compile(model)
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=6e-4, betas=(0.9, 0.95), weight_decay=0.1)

for step, (x, y) in enumerate(loader):
    with torch.autocast("cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16):
        logits = model(x)
        loss = torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)), y.view(-1))
    loss.backward()
    torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    for g in opt.param_groups:
        g["lr"] = lr_schedule(step)
    opt.step()
    opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)

Sanity checks before scaling up:

  • Initial loss should be about ln(vocabulary size) (around 10.8 for GPT-2's 50,257-token vocabulary).
  • The model should overfit one small batch to near-zero loss.
  • Loss should decrease smoothly on a tiny run.
  • Checkpoint saving and resuming must work exactly.

See gradient descent and backpropagation and mixed precision training.

Step 9: Evaluate and deploy

  • Held-out validation loss on your data.
  • Benchmarks with EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness: HellaSwag, ARC, MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval. See AI benchmarks explained.
  • Human evaluation for your use case.
  • Safety evaluation.
  • Deploy: convert to GGUF or serve with vLLM; quantize for efficiency. See run an LLM locally and LLM quantization.

Tools and frameworks

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to train an LLM from scratch?

From about $20 for a 124M toy model to hundreds of thousands of dollars for a 7B model and tens or hundreds of millions for frontier models, mostly depending on parameters × tokens.

Can I train an LLM on my own computer?

Yes, small models (up to a few hundred million parameters) on a single high-end GPU. Larger models need cloud clusters.

How much data do I need to train an LLM?

At least about 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training; modern small models use far more.

How long does it take to train an LLM?

Hours for tiny models, days to weeks for 1–7B models on GPU clusters, and months for frontier models.

Is it better to train from scratch or fine-tune?

Fine-tuning is better for most applications. Train from scratch to learn, research new methods, or when you need full control over data.

content:
Short answer

The Jetson Orin Nano Super is NVIDIA's $249 developer kit for edge AI, launched in December 2024. It delivers up to 67 INT8 TOPS (sparse) from an Ampere GPU with 1,024 CUDA cores and 32 tensor cores, a 6-core Arm CPU and 8 GB of LPDDR5 memory at 102 GB/s, in a power envelope up to 25 W. It is excellent for computer vision, robotics, speech and small language models up to about 4–8 billion parameters at 4-bit quantization. Its memory bandwidth limits an 8B model to roughly 15–20 tokens per second at best, so it is not a substitute for a desktop GPU for large LLMs, but it is the most affordable way to build CUDA-powered AI devices.

Specifications

"Super" is mostly software: NVIDIA's JetPack update raised clocks and power limits (the 25 W mode), increasing AI performance by up to 1.7× for generative AI and memory bandwidth by about 50% over the original Orin Nano. Existing Orin Nano developer kits can be upgraded with the software update.

What does 67 TOPS mean?

TOPS counts INT8 operations per second, and NVIDIA's figure assumes sparsity. It is useful for comparing vision inference with quantized models, but for language models the memory bandwidth (102 GB/s) usually matters more. See TOPS vs TFLOPS and GPU memory bandwidth.

Which AI models fit in 8 GB?

Memory is shared between the operating system, CPU and GPU, so plan for roughly 5–6 GB for models.

Larger models (13B+) generally won't fit. Demonstrations of 70B models streamed from SSD exist, but they run at one token per minutes, which is not practical.

Realistic LLM speed

Single-user token generation is limited by bandwidth:

max tokens/s ≈ 102 GB/s ÷ model size in memory

Prompt processing (reading long inputs) is compute-bound and slower than on desktop GPUs. For context, see prefill vs decode.

Software stack

Setup and optimisation tips

1. Flash the latest JetPack using NVIDIA's SD card image or SDK Manager. 2. Enable the 25 W Super mode (sudo nvpmodel -m <mode> and sudo jetson_clocks). 3. Use an NVMe SSD instead of microSD for speed and swap space. 4. Quantize models to 4-bit (Q4_K_M GGUF) or INT8/FP16 TensorRT engines. 5. Free memory: run headless (no desktop), stop unused services and containers. 6. Cooling: the dev kit includes a fan; keep it unobstructed in Super mode. 7. Monitor with tegrastats or jtop.

Project ideas

  • Offline voice assistant (Whisper + small LLM + Piper TTS).
  • Smart security camera with object detection and alerts.
  • Robot with vision-language navigation.
  • Private home-automation assistant.
  • Wildlife or traffic monitoring.
  • Educational CUDA and AI learning platform.

See What is edge AI? and What is computer vision?

Jetson Orin Nano Super vs alternatives

Who should buy it?

Buy it if you want to learn CUDA and edge AI, build robots or smart cameras, or run small private AI assistants on a low power budget.

Skip it if your main goal is running large language models quickly; a used RTX 3090 PC, a Mac with more memory or an AMD Strix Halo mini PC is far better. See best GPU for local LLMs and Ryzen AI Max+ 395 for LLMs.

Frequently asked questions

Can the Jetson Orin Nano Super run LLMs?

Yes, small models up to about 4B run well, and 7–8B models run at 4-bit with modest speed (roughly 12–18 tokens/s).

What is the difference between Jetson Orin Nano and Orin Nano Super?

The Super is the same hardware with a software update enabling higher clocks and a 25 W mode, giving up to 1.7× faster generative AI performance, at a lower $249 price for the dev kit.

Does the Jetson Orin Nano Super have CUDA and tensor cores?

Yes: 1,024 CUDA cores and 32 third-generation tensor cores on an Ampere GPU. See how tensor cores work.

How much power does it use?

Between 7 W and 25 W depending on the power mode.

Is it better than a Raspberry Pi for AI?

For GPU-accelerated AI, CUDA and language models, yes. A Raspberry Pi with an AI HAT is cheaper for simple vision tasks.

The GH100 chip

Like most large GPUs, H100 ships with some units disabled to improve manufacturing yield. See how a GPU works.

What the specs mean

TFLOPS and sparsity

NVIDIA's headline tensor figures assume 2:4 structured sparsity, where half the weights are zero in a specific pattern. Most real AI workloads run dense, so use the dense numbers (half the headline) when estimating performance. See structured sparsity explained and how to read a GPU spec sheet.

Precisions

H100 was the first NVIDIA GPU with FP8 tensor cores. It does not support FP4, which arrived with Blackwell. See precision formats and mixed precision training.

Memory and bandwidth

For large language model inference, memory bandwidth usually limits token generation speed, and capacity limits model size. A rough single-user ceiling is bandwidth ÷ model size in bytes: an 8B model in FP8 (about 8 GB) on H100 SXM could reach about 3,350 ÷ 8 ≈ 400 tokens/s at best. See GPU memory bandwidth and how much VRAM for an LLM.

NVLink and NVSwitch

H100 SXM uses fourth-generation NVLink with 18 links for 900 GB/s total bandwidth per GPU, about 7× PCIe Gen5. In an HGX H100 board, eight GPUs connect through NVSwitch so any GPU talks to any other at full speed. See NVLink and NVSwitch explained.

MIG (Multi-Instance GPU)

MIG splits one H100 into up to seven isolated GPUs, each with its own memory and compute, useful for serving many small models or sharing in the cloud.

New features in Hopper

See how tensor cores work, tensor core generations and FlashAttention explained.

H100 SXM vs PCIe vs NVL: which is which?

Full comparison: H100 PCIe vs SXM.

H100 compared with other NVIDIA data center GPUs

Real-world performance

  • Training: H100 typically trains large transformers around 2–3× faster than A100 in BF16, more with FP8.
  • Utilisation: well-optimised training reaches roughly 35–50% of dense peak (MFU). See MFU explained.
  • Inference: FP8 with TensorRT-LLM, vLLM or SGLang gives large gains over A100. See LLM inference engines compared.

Power and systems

  • An HGX/DGX H100 server has 8 GPUs (640 GB total) and draws around 10 kW.
  • Most H100 SXM systems are air-cooled; liquid-cooled versions exist.

How much memory does the H100 have?

80 GB for the SXM (HBM3) and PCIe (HBM2e) versions, and 94 GB HBM3 for the H100 NVL.

How many TFLOPS is the H100?

The H100 SXM delivers 989 TFLOPS dense BF16/FP16 and 1,979 TFLOPS dense FP8 on tensor cores (double with sparsity), plus 67 TFLOPS FP32.

Up to 700 W for SXM, 300–350 W for PCIe and 350–400 W for NVL.

Does the H100 support FP4?

No. FP4 tensor core support arrived with Blackwell (B200, B300, RTX 50 series).

Can you use an H100 for gaming?

No. It has no display outputs and lacks the graphics features of GeForce cards.

Is the H100 still worth it in 2026?

Yes for many workloads. Prices have fallen as Blackwell ships, making H100 strong value for training and inference of models that fit in 80 GB.

META: Ollama vs LM Studio compared: features, speed, MLX on Mac, APIs, licensing, hardware support and which local LLM tool suits beginners or developers.
EXCERPT: Ollama and LM Studio are the two most popular ways to run AI models on your own computer. A detailed comparison: interface, installation, model libraries, performance on NVIDIA, AMD and Apple Silicon, APIs and integrations, server use, licensing, privacy, a feature-by-feature table, step-by-step quick starts and clear recommendations.

Both are free, both run GGUF models through llama.cpp-based engines, both offer an OpenAI-compatible API (Ollama on port 11434, LM Studio on port 1234), and both support NVIDIA, AMD and Apple hardware. content:
Short answer

In the Ollama vs LM Studio choice, the short answer is: LM Studio is the easiest desktop app for exploring and chatting with local models, with a built-in Hugging Face model browser and MLX acceleration on Apple Silicon; Ollama is the best choice for developers and servers thanks to its simple command line, background service, official Docker image and huge integration ecosystem. Both are free, both run GGUF models through llama.cpp-based engines, both offer an OpenAI-compatible API (Ollama on port 11434, LM Studio on port 1234), and both support NVIDIA, AMD and Apple hardware. Ollama is open source (MIT); LM Studio is free for personal and work use but closed source. Many people install both.

Quick comparison

What is Ollama?

Ollama is an open-source tool that downloads and runs LLMs with one command:

ollama run qwen3:8b

It runs as a background service, exposing a local API that apps, IDE extensions, agents and web UIs (such as Open WebUI) can use. Models are configured with a Modelfile, similar to a Dockerfile. Ollama also offers optional cloud-hosted models for larger sizes, but local use requires no account.

What is LM Studio?

LM Studio is a desktop application for discovering, downloading and chatting with local models. It shows which quantizations fit your hardware, supports document chat (RAG), and can start a local server with one click. On Macs it uses Apple's MLX framework by default, which is often faster than llama.cpp on Apple Silicon. Its lms command-line tool and SDKs let developers script it.

Installation and first run

Ollama

1. Download from ollama.com (or curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh on Linux). 2. Run ollama run <model> in a terminal, or open the desktop app. 3. Use the API at http://localhost:11434.

LM Studio

1. Download from lmstudio.ai. 2. Search for a model, choose a quantization marked as fitting your memory, click download. 3. Chat in the app, or enable the local server at http://localhost:1234.

Performance

Both tools use similar underlying inference engines, so on the same backend, speed is usually similar.

For heavy multi-user serving, neither is the fastest option; consider vLLM or SGLang. See LLM inference engines compared.

Models and quantization

See LLM quantization explained and best open source LLMs to run locally.

API and integrations

Both expose OpenAI-compatible endpoints, so most apps can switch by changing the base URL:

from openai import OpenAI

# Ollama
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1", api_key="ollama")
# LM Studio
# client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:1234/v1", api_key="lm-studio")

r = client.chat.completions.create(model="qwen3:8b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain tensor cores in one sentence."}])
print(r.choices[0].message.content)

Ollama has broader built-in support across third-party tools (Open WebUI, Continue, LangChain, LlamaIndex, n8n, many coding agents), largely because it was designed as a service. LM Studio is catching up with its SDKs and MCP support.

Privacy and security

  • Both run models locally; prompts stay on your machine unless you use cloud features.
  • Don't expose either server to the internet without authentication: by default they listen on localhost. Binding Ollama to 0.0.0.0 on a public machine without a firewall or proxy has led to exposed instances.
  • Ollama being open source means its code can be audited; LM Studio's app is closed source.

Licensing and commercial use

  • Ollama: MIT licence, free for any use.
  • LM Studio: free for home and work use under its terms; check the current terms for redistribution or enterprise features.
  • Models have their own licences (Apache 2.0, MIT, Llama licence, Gemma terms and so on), regardless of the tool.

Which should you choose?

Using both: many people explore models in LM Studio, then run their favourites through Ollama for integrations.

Alternatives

Hardware tips

  • NVIDIA: 16–24 GB VRAM covers most popular models; see best GPU for local LLMs.
  • Mac: unified memory decides model size; see best Mac for local LLMs.
  • AMD: check ROCm support or use Vulkan; see ROCm vs CUDA.
  • Use the VRAM calculator before downloading.

Frequently asked questions

Is Ollama faster than LM Studio?

On NVIDIA GPUs they are usually similar. On Apple Silicon, LM Studio with MLX is often faster. Ollama uses less memory when idle.

Is LM Studio free for commercial use?

LM Studio is free for home and work use under its current terms. Check its website for the latest licensing details.

Can I use Ollama models in LM Studio?

Not directly from Ollama's storage format, but both use GGUF files, so you can download the same models for each tool.

Which is better for beginners?

LM Studio, thanks to its graphical model browser and chat interface.

Can Ollama and LM Studio run at the same time?

Yes, they use different ports (11434 and 1234), but running large models in both will compete for memory.

content:
Short answer

ROCm vs CUDA is the software side of the AMD vs NVIDIA battle. CUDA, launched by NVIDIA in 2007, is the most mature GPU computing platform, with nearly two decades of libraries, tools and community support. ROCm is AMD's open-source alternative; its HIP programming model mirrors CUDA closely, so much CUDA code can be ported with tools like HIPIFY. In 2026, PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang, Triton and llama.cpp all run on ROCm, and AMD's Instinct MI300X, MI325X and MI355X accelerators are competitive on many inference workloads, often at lower prices. CUDA still leads in ecosystem breadth, out-of-the-box reliability, consumer GPU support and highly optimised kernels. Choose CUDA for the smoothest path; consider ROCm when price, memory capacity or vendor diversity matter.

What are CUDA and ROCm?

See What is CUDA? and AMD vs NVIDIA for AI.

The software stacks side by side

Framework and tool support (2026)

The broad pattern: mainstream workflows now work on ROCm, but cutting-edge research code, custom kernels and niche libraries often appear on CUDA first. See LLM inference engines compared and Triton.

Supported hardware

Practical point: almost any NVIDIA GPU runs CUDA, while ROCm officially supports a narrower list. Check AMD's compatibility matrix before buying a Radeon card for AI.

Performance: what the evidence shows

Performance depends heavily on software version and workload.

Independent analyses in 2024 (for example by SemiAnalysis) found AMD's hardware had strong specifications but its training software lagged; AMD responded with faster ROCm releases and closer work with framework developers. More recent comparisons report a much smaller gap for inference.

Hardware specs matter too:

AMD's memory advantage lets large models fit on fewer GPUs. See MI355X vs B200 and NVIDIA H100 specs.

Cloud pricing

On our GPU cloud price tracker (November 27, 2026), typical on-demand prices were about $3.43/hour for MI300X (lowest around $2.89) versus a $3.92 median for H100 and $4.95 for H200. Fewer providers offer AMD GPUs, which affects availability. See cloud GPU providers compared.

Porting CUDA code to ROCm

HIP mirrors CUDA's API:

Steps:

1. Run hipify-perl or hipify-clang to convert source files. 2. Replace CUDA libraries with ROCm equivalents (cuBLAS → hipBLAS, NCCL → RCCL). 3. Compile with hipcc. 4. Profile and tune: AMD GPUs use 64-thread wavefronts on Instinct (CUDA warps are 32 threads), and differ in shared memory (LDS) and cache, so tuned CUDA kernels may need adjustment.

HIP code can also compile for NVIDIA GPUs, allowing a single codebase. See your first CUDA kernel.

Using ROCm at home

For running models locally, see run an LLM locally and Ryzen AI Max+ 395 for local LLMs.

Why CUDA's lead persists

1. Time: nearly two decades of development and optimisation. 2. Ecosystem: most AI research code is written and tested on NVIDIA first. 3. Libraries: cuDNN, cuBLAS, NCCL, TensorRT and CUTLASS are deeply optimised. 4. Developer familiarity: universities and companies train on CUDA. 5. Hardware availability: NVIDIA GPUs are everywhere, from laptops to supercomputers.

Why ROCm is gaining ground

1. Open source: inspectable and modifiable. 2. Cost and supply: buyers want a second source. 3. Memory capacity: MI300-series GPUs offer more HBM per GPU. 4. Framework abstraction: PyTorch, Triton and vLLM hide much of the hardware difference. 5. Big customers: large AI companies and cloud providers have deployed AMD Instinct GPUs at scale.

Which should you choose?

Frequently asked questions

Is ROCm as good as CUDA?

For mainstream PyTorch and LLM inference on supported AMD GPUs, ROCm is now capable and often competitive. CUDA remains more mature, broader and easier.

Can CUDA code run on AMD GPUs?

Not directly, but HIPIFY can convert most CUDA code to HIP, which runs on AMD GPUs (and can also compile for NVIDIA).

Does ROCm work on Windows?

ROCm support on Windows is more limited than on Linux; PyTorch ROCm on Windows has been in preview. Many Windows users run local LLMs on Radeon GPUs through Vulkan-based tools.

Does PyTorch support AMD GPUs?

Yes. PyTorch provides official ROCm builds for Linux, and the same torch.cuda API calls work on AMD GPUs.

Is AMD cheaper than NVIDIA for AI?

Often, per GB of memory and sometimes per token served, but total cost depends on software efficiency, engineering time and availability.

content:
Short answer

The link between superintelligence and climate change cuts both ways. Optimists, including OpenAI's Sam Altman, argue that superintelligence could help fix the climate by discovering better batteries, cheaper clean energy, new materials and fusion power. Critics point out that we already have most of the technology needed to cut emissions; what is missing is policy, money and political will, and AI itself is adding fast-growing electricity demand. The realistic picture: superintelligence could speed up innovation and lower the cost of decarbonisation, but it cannot by itself build power lines, pass carbon prices or overcome local opposition, and its own energy footprint must be powered cleanly.

Two opposing views

Both sides contain truth. The useful question is not "will AI solve climate change?" but "which parts of the climate problem are limited by intelligence?"

What AI already does for climate (before superintelligence)

The 2019 paper "Tackling Climate Change with Machine Learning" (Rolnick et al.) mapped dozens of such applications. See AI scientific discovery.

What superintelligence could add

1. Faster clean-energy breakthroughs

2. Smarter infrastructure planning

Superintelligent planning could design grids, transmission routes, storage and demand response for entire continents, potentially lowering costs substantially.

3. Better climate science

More accurate regional climate projections, earlier warnings of tipping points, and improved understanding of clouds and ice sheets, two of the biggest uncertainties in climate models.

4. Economic and policy design

Superintelligence could model the effects of carbon pricing, subsidies and trade policies in detail. However, choosing and implementing policy remains a human political decision.

5. Automated labour

Combined with robotics, advanced AI could reduce the cost of building solar farms, retrofitting buildings and manufacturing equipment, which addresses a real bottleneck: skilled labour.

What superintelligence cannot easily fix

As MIT Technology Review argued in 2024, intelligence is necessary but not sufficient: technology breakthroughs help, but policy changes are still required.

The other side: AI's energy footprint

The race toward superintelligence requires enormous computing power.

  • The International Energy Agency's *Energy and AI* report (2025) projected data center electricity demand roughly doubling by 2030, with AI the main driver.
  • Single AI campuses are being planned at gigawatt scale, comparable to large power plants.
  • Some new demand is being met by natural gas, which increases emissions, while tech companies also sign large deals for nuclear, solar, wind and geothermal power.

See AI energy consumption, liquid cooling for AI data centers and superintelligence compute requirements.

A realistic scorecard

Risks specific to superintelligence and climate

1. Delay through techno-optimism: waiting for AI to solve climate could reduce urgency for actions available today. 2. Geoengineering decisions: a powerful AI might recommend solar radiation management; who decides whether to deploy it? 3. Misaligned optimisation: an AI told to "reduce emissions" without proper constraints could propose harmful solutions. See the control problem and AI alignment. 4. Concentration of benefits: breakthroughs owned by a few companies or countries may not reach poorer nations most affected by warming. See superintelligence geopolitics.

What would make superintelligence good for the climate

  • Power AI data centers with additional clean energy, not displaced clean energy.
  • Direct AI research toward climate-critical science: storage, materials, grids and agriculture.
  • Share breakthroughs widely, including with developing countries.
  • Keep implementing proven climate policies now rather than waiting.
  • Govern advanced AI safely so its benefits can be realised. See superintelligence governance.

Frequently asked questions

Can superintelligence solve climate change?

It could accelerate solutions significantly, especially in materials, energy and planning, but deployment depends on policy, investment and physical construction that intelligence alone cannot deliver.

Is AI bad for the climate?

AI increases electricity demand, and some of that is met with fossil fuels. Whether AI is net positive depends on how it is powered and used.

Which is the bigger threat: AI or climate change?

Experts disagree. Climate change is causing harm now; risks from advanced AI are more uncertain but could be severe. Many researchers argue both deserve serious attention.

Will superintelligence invent fusion power?

It might accelerate fusion research, particularly plasma control and reactor design, but building and testing reactors still takes years.

Short answer

Superintelligence and education raise a question schools have never faced: what should people learn when machines can know and reason better than any human expert? Today's AI tutors already show promising results, including a 2024 Harvard physics study in which students using a carefully designed AI tutor learned more than twice as much in less time than in an active-learning class. Superintelligence could make world-class personalised tutoring free for everyone, transform assessment, and shift the purpose of education from memorising knowledge to judgement, collaboration, character, creativity and meaning. The risks are real too: over-reliance that weakens thinking, cheating, inequality, surveillance and loss of human connection. The best preparation now is to learn deeply with AI, not just outsource work to it.

Why superintelligence changes the purpose of education

Modern schooling has three main jobs:

1. Transmit knowledge and skills needed for work and citizenship. 2. Sort and certify people through grades and degrees. 3. Socialise and develop young people: character, friendships, civic values and childcare.

Superintelligence affects each very differently:

Education researcher Rose Luckin argued as early as 2018 that education must shift from a "knowledge-based curriculum" toward developing the full range of human intelligence, including self-knowledge and social intelligence.

What the evidence says about AI tutoring today

The lesson: AI helps learning when it is designed to make students think (hints, questions, feedback) and harms learning when it simply does the work. See How does ChatGPT work?

How education could change in stages

See When will AGI arrive? and AGI vs ASI.

What a superintelligent tutor could do

  • Perfect personalisation: know exactly what each student understands and what confuses them.
  • Infinite patience: explain a concept 50 different ways without frustration.
  • Every language and level: teach advanced physics in Urdu, Swahili or sign language.
  • Multimodal teaching: simulations, interactive experiments and visual explanations. See multimodal AI.
  • Motivation: adapt to interests, connecting maths to football or music.
  • Accessibility: support learners with disabilities in highly tailored ways.
  • Learning science built in: spaced repetition, retrieval practice and metacognition by default.

Skills that stay valuable in an age of superintelligence

For how jobs could change, see jobs at risk from superintelligence.

Major risks

1. Cognitive outsourcing

If students let AI think for them, they may not develop the skills needed to understand or supervise AI. "Desirable difficulty" (struggling productively) is central to learning.

2. Cheating and broken assessment

Take-home essays and online tests become unreliable. Schools are already shifting to in-class writing, oral exams, projects and process-based grading.

3. Inequality

Wealthy students may get the best AI tools plus human mentors, while poorer schools get only cheap chatbots. Alternatively, free AI tutors could narrow gaps dramatically. Policy choices will decide.

4. Surveillance and privacy

AI tutors collect detailed data on how children think and feel. Who owns it, and how is it used?

5. Homogenisation

If everyone learns from the same few AI systems, diversity of thought and culture could shrink.

6. Loss of human connection

Teachers inspire, care and model values. Over-automating education could harm children's social and emotional development.

7. Persuasion and manipulation

A superintelligent tutor could shape beliefs very effectively. Alignment and oversight matter. See What is AI alignment?

What happens to universities?

Practical advice now

For students

  • Use AI as a tutor, not a ghostwriter: ask it to quiz you, explain mistakes and give hints.
  • Try problems yourself first, then compare with AI.
  • Learn fundamentals deeply, especially maths, writing and reasoning.
  • Build real projects and a portfolio.
  • Learn how AI works; start with what is an LLM and prompt engineering.

For parents

  • Encourage curiosity and reading over grades alone.
  • Watch for over-reliance; ask children to explain what they learned.
  • Value social, physical and creative activities.

For teachers

  • Redesign assessment around in-class work, oral explanation and projects.
  • Use AI to reduce administrative work and personalise practice.
  • Teach AI literacy and verification.
  • Focus your unique value: mentorship, motivation and community.

For policymakers

  • Fund research on what AI tutoring designs actually improve learning.
  • Provide equal access to high-quality AI tools.
  • Protect student data.
  • Update curricula and qualifications.
  • Support lifelong learning and retraining.

Education after superintelligence: what is learning for?

If superintelligence does most economically valuable thinking, education may return to older ideals: learning for its own sake, understanding the world, becoming a good person and participating in democracy. Philosophy, history, art, sport and science could flourish as sources of meaning rather than career preparation. See meaning of life after superintelligence and what happens after superintelligence.

Frequently asked questions

Will AI replace teachers?

AI will likely take over much content delivery and grading, but human teachers remain important for motivation, mentoring, social development and supervision, especially for children.

Is it still worth going to university?

For now, yes, especially for fields with hands-on work, strong networks or regulated professions. The value of degrees as job signals may decline as AI advances.

What should children learn for a world with superintelligence?

Strong fundamentals, critical thinking, communication, collaboration, creativity, ethics, practical skills and how to learn and use AI responsibly.

Does using ChatGPT make students worse learners?

It depends on how it is used. Answer-copying can reduce learning; guided tutoring that makes students think can improve it.

  • Rose Luckin, The future is super intelligent, not artificially intelligent, and education must respond (UCL IOE, 2018)
  • UNESCO, Guidance for generative AI in education and research (2023)

content:
Short answer

Superintelligence governance means the rules, institutions and agreements that would control the development of AI far smarter than humans. Proposals range from an "IAEA for AI" (suggested by OpenAI's leaders in 2023) that would inspect and license systems above a compute threshold, to the October 2025 Superintelligence Statement calling for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there is broad scientific consensus it can be done safely and strong public buy-in. Existing laws such as the EU AI Act cover general-purpose AI but not superintelligence specifically. Because training frontier AI needs huge numbers of specialised chips, compute governance (tracking chips, data centers and training runs) is widely seen as the most practical lever. The hardest problems are international coordination, verification and acting before capabilities arrive.

Why governing superintelligence is uniquely hard

The main governance proposals

What already exists (as of late 2026)

See the Superintelligence Statement.

Compute governance: the most practical lever

Training frontier AI requires tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs, made by a handful of companies using a handful of factories. That makes compute unusually governable:

Limits: algorithmic progress means the compute needed for a given capability falls over time, so thresholds must adapt. Inference compute and distributed training also complicate monitoring. See superintelligence compute requirements, AI chip shortage and our GPU price tracker.

Verification: the hardest technical problem

Any international agreement needs ways to check compliance:

  • Data center monitoring: satellite imagery and power consumption can reveal large facilities.
  • Chip tracking: serial numbers, supply chain audits and possibly on-chip attestation.
  • Model evaluations: third-party testing of dangerous capabilities.
  • Whistleblower protections: insiders often know first.
  • Inspections: an international inspectorate, like nuclear inspectors.

Nuclear arms control shows verification is possible but slow to build and politically fragile.

Governing the transition, not just the technology

Governance is not only about preventing catastrophe. It also concerns:

  • Distribution of benefits: who gets the wealth superintelligence creates? See superintelligence economics.
  • Jobs and social stability: see jobs at risk from superintelligence.
  • Democratic legitimacy: who decides what values superintelligence follows?
  • Rights of AI systems: if AI becomes conscious, does it have moral status? See can superintelligence be conscious?

Arguments against strict superintelligence regulation

  • Innovation and benefits: delays could postpone cures and economic growth.
  • Competition: unilateral restrictions might hand leadership to less careful actors.
  • Uncertainty: regulating hypothetical systems may produce poorly designed rules.
  • Regulatory capture: big labs could use regulation to block startups and open-source developers.
  • Feasibility: a global ban may be impossible to enforce.

These concerns are serious, which is why many proposals focus on thresholds that affect only the most powerful systems.

A realistic roadmap

What you can do

  • Follow and contribute to public consultations on AI law.
  • Support AI literacy so citizens can participate in decisions; see what is superintelligence?
  • For technical people: work on evaluations, interpretability and alignment; see AI alignment.

Frequently asked questions

Is superintelligence regulated anywhere?

No law specifically regulates superintelligence. The EU AI Act and some national laws regulate the most capable general-purpose models, which is a partial step.

What is an "IAEA for AI"?

An international body, modelled on the International Atomic Energy Agency, that could inspect AI developers, audit systems and enforce safety standards above certain capability thresholds.

Can a global ban on superintelligence work?

It would require cooperation among major AI powers and robust verification. Supporters say it is necessary; critics say it is unenforceable. Compute governance would likely be central to any attempt.

Who signed the Superintelligence Statement?

It was signed by many scientists, including AI pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, alongside public figures from different fields and political backgrounds.

What is compute governance?

Using control over AI chips, data centers and training runs to monitor and regulate the development of powerful AI.

Short answer

Superintelligence vs human brain comparisons start with one striking fact: the brain runs general intelligence on about 20 watts, while a single NVIDIA H100 GPU draws up to 700 watts and frontier AI training clusters draw tens to hundreds of megawatts. The brain has about 86 billion neurons and roughly 100 trillion synapses; leading estimates put its computation at around 1013 to 1017 operations per second, with about 1015 a common central figure. A single modern GPU already exceeds that range in raw operations, so the remaining advantages of the brain are energy efficiency, learning from little data and architecture, not raw speed. Machines, meanwhile, win on speed, copying, memory precision and scale, which is why many researchers believe superintelligence is physically achievable.

Side-by-side comparison

How much compute does the brain have?

There is no single answer because neurons are not digital processors. Researchers use several methods:

Joe Carlsmith's 2020 report for Open Philanthropy concluded that about 1015 FLOP/s is likely enough to match the brain's task performance, with 1013–1017 plausible. That central figure is roughly the dense FP16 throughput of a single H100.

What this means: raw compute is no longer the main gap. A single data center holds hundreds of thousands of brain-equivalents of operations per second. The question is whether we have the right algorithms. See superintelligence compute requirements.

Energy: the brain's biggest advantage

On these rough numbers, the brain is still around 10 to 40 times more energy-efficient than the best AI chips per operation, and far more efficient when you count the whole data center (cooling, networking, memory). The comparison is imprecise, but the direction is clear. A 2023 paper in *Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence* by Stiefel and Coggan argued that brute-force simulation of brains on today's chips would be enormously energy-hungry, which is why efficiency research matters. See AI energy consumption and GPU power consumption.

Why is the brain so efficient?

  • Sparse activity: only a small fraction of neurons fire at any moment.
  • Memory and compute together: synapses store and process information in the same place, avoiding the energy cost of moving data. In chips, moving data from memory often costs more energy than computing on it. See GPU memory bandwidth.
  • Low voltage, slow, analogue-like signalling.
  • Evolutionary optimisation over hundreds of millions of years.

Speed: machines win decisively

Neurons fire at most a few hundred times per second. Transistors switch at gigahertz frequencies, millions of times faster. An AI model can read a book in seconds and generate thousands of words per minute. If a system matched human reasoning quality but ran 100 times faster, it would already be a form of "speed superintelligence," as Nick Bostrom describes it. See superintelligence explained.

Memory and knowledge

Learning efficiency: where humans still lead

A human child reaches fluent language after hearing perhaps tens of millions of words. Frontier language models train on tens of trillions of tokens, roughly a million times more text. Humans also learn new skills from a handful of examples and transfer knowledge across domains easily. Closing this sample-efficiency gap is a major research goal, and it is one reason some researchers believe current methods need new ideas to reach superintelligence. See how to achieve superintelligence.

Architecture: different designs, different strengths

Neuromorphic chips (such as Intel's Loihi research chips and IBM's NorthPole) try to borrow brain-like features for efficiency, but GPUs remain dominant for AI.

Will AI surpass the brain?

Machines already surpass humans in specific domains: calculation, games like Go, protein structure prediction and increasingly coding and mathematics. General superiority requires:

1. Algorithms that learn and reason as flexibly as humans. 2. Enough compute, which appears available at data center scale. 3. Energy and infrastructure, which is the main physical bottleneck. 4. Data, including learning from interaction rather than only text.

Because hardware can scale beyond any biological limit (a data center can be the size of many football fields and draw a gigawatt), once algorithms match the brain's efficiency, scale could push AI far beyond human capability. That is the core argument behind the intelligence explosion.

Common misconceptions

  • "We use only 10% of our brains." False; nearly all brain regions are active over a day.
  • "Parameters equal synapses." Not directly; a synapse is far more complex than a single number, and a parameter is far simpler.
  • "More FLOPs automatically mean more intelligence." Compute is necessary but algorithms matter enormously.
  • "The brain is a computer." It processes information, but its design differs fundamentally from digital computers.

Frequently asked questions

How many FLOPS is the human brain?

Estimates range from about 1013 to 1017 FLOP/s, with around 1015 FLOP/s a widely cited central estimate.

Is a GPU faster than the human brain?

In raw arithmetic operations, a modern data center GPU is in the same range or above common brain estimates, but it uses about 35–50 times more power and lacks the brain's learning abilities.

How much energy does the brain use?

Around 20 watts, roughly 20% of the body's resting energy use, despite being about 2% of body weight.

Could a superintelligence run on 20 watts?

In principle physics allows very efficient computation, as the brain demonstrates, but no current AI approach is close to that efficiency for general intelligence.

Will AI ever be conscious like a brain?

This is an open question in philosophy and neuroscience. See Can superintelligence be conscious?

  • Stiefel & Coggan, The energy challenges of artificial superintelligence (*Frontiers in AI*, 2023)
  • AI Impacts, Brain performance in TEPS (reported by IEEE Spectrum, 2015)

content:
Short answer

What is LoRA? LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a technique for fine-tuning large AI models cheaply. Instead of updating all of a model's billions of weights, LoRA freezes the original model and trains two small matrices per layer whose product represents the change. Introduced by Microsoft researchers (Hu et al.) in 2021, it cut trainable parameters for GPT-3 175B by about 10,000× and GPU memory by about 3×, with quality comparable to full fine-tuning. Typical LoRA adapters are just megabytes to a few hundred megabytes, can be swapped like plugins, and add no inference latency once merged. Combined with 4-bit quantization (QLoRA), you can fine-tune an 8B model on a single consumer GPU with about 8–12 GB of VRAM.

Why LoRA exists

Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model to a task or style. Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which is expensive:

  • Memory: with the Adam optimizer in mixed precision, full fine-tuning needs roughly 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients and optimizer states), so an 8B model needs over 120 GB before activations.
  • Storage: every fine-tuned version is a full copy of the model.
  • Compute: updating all weights is slow.

LoRA's insight: the *change* needed to adapt a model usually has a low "intrinsic rank," so it can be represented with far fewer numbers.

How LoRA works

For a weight matrix W (size d × k), LoRA learns an update ΔW = B·A, where:

  • A has size r × k
  • B has size d × r
  • r (the rank) is small, typically 8–64

The layer's output becomes:

h = W·x + (alpha / r) · B·A·x
  • W stays frozen.
  • B is initialised to zero, so training starts from the original model's behaviour.
  • alpha scales the update.
  • After training, B·A can be merged into W, so inference speed is unchanged.

Worked example: how many parameters?

For one attention projection with d = k = 4,096:

Applied across all attention and MLP layers of an 8B model, LoRA at r = 16 typically trains roughly 0.5% of parameters, tens of millions instead of billions.

LoRA vs other fine-tuning methods

Other variants include rsLoRA (better scaling at high ranks), LoRA+ (different learning rates for A and B), PiSSA (initialising from principal components) and VeRA (even fewer parameters).

QLoRA: fine-tuning big models on small GPUs

QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) combines LoRA with a 4-bit quantized base model. Its key ideas:

  • NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat) data type designed for normally distributed weights.
  • Double quantization of the quantization constants to save more memory.
  • Paged optimizers to handle memory spikes.

The paper showed a 65B model could be fine-tuned on a single 48 GB GPU. See LLM quantization explained.

How much VRAM do you need?

Approximate requirements for fine-tuning with a short sequence length (around 2K tokens), batch size 1–2 and gradient checkpointing. Longer sequences and bigger batches need more.

Use our VRAM calculator for inference sizing and see best GPU for deep learning. Renting is often easiest for one-off runs; see the GPU cloud price tracker.

Recommended LoRA hyperparameters

Example: LoRA with Hugging Face PEFT

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model

model_id = "your-base-model"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, torch_dtype="bfloat16", device_map="auto")

config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,
    lora_alpha=32,
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj", "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"],
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
model = get_peft_model(model, config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# then train with the Trainer or TRL's SFTTrainer

For QLoRA, load the model with BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4") and call prepare_model_for_kbit_training before adding the adapter.

After training, merge for deployment:

model = model.merge_and_unload()
model.save_pretrained("merged-model")

Tools for LoRA fine-tuning

LoRA for image models

LoRA is hugely popular for Stable Diffusion and FLUX, where small adapters teach a model a new character, object or style from a few dozen images. Image LoRAs are often only 10–200 MB and can be combined with weighting. See What is a diffusion model? and best GPU for Stable Diffusion.

Serving many LoRAs efficiently

Because adapters are small, one base model can serve many customers or tasks. Inference engines such as vLLM and SGLang support multi-LoRA serving, loading different adapters per request. See LLM inference engines compared.

When LoRA is not enough

  • Teaching large amounts of new knowledge (LoRA is better at style, format and behaviour than memorising facts; consider RAG).
  • Major changes such as a new language or modality may benefit from higher ranks or full fine-tuning.
  • Very small datasets may overfit; quality data matters more than settings.

Common mistakes

1. Learning rate too low (copying full fine-tuning values). 2. Targeting only attention layers when all linear layers work better. 3. Wrong chat template during training versus inference. 4. Training too long and overfitting. 5. Poor data: a few hundred high-quality examples often beat thousands of noisy ones. 6. Forgetting to evaluate against the base model.

Frequently asked questions

What does LoRA stand for?

Low-Rank Adaptation, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method introduced in the 2021 paper "LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models."

Is LoRA as good as full fine-tuning?

For most instruction tuning and style adaptation tasks, LoRA gets close. Full fine-tuning can still win when learning large amounts of new information.

What rank should I use for LoRA?

Start with r = 16 and alpha = 16–32. Increase rank for complex tasks or large datasets.

Can I fine-tune a 70B model with LoRA on one GPU?

With QLoRA, yes, on a GPU with roughly 48 GB or more (for example, an RTX PRO 6000 or H100), at short sequence lengths.

Does LoRA slow down inference?

Not once merged into the base weights. Unmerged adapters add a small overhead.

Sources and further reading

  • Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models (2021)
  • Dettmers et al., QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (2023)
  • Liu et al., DoRA: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (2024)
  • Hugging Face, PEFT documentation
  • IBM, What is LoRA?

KEY: The technological singularity is the hypothetical moment when artificial intelligence becomes capable of improving itself faster than humans can follow, triggering runaway technological change that makes the future impossible to predict. The idea traces back to John von Neumann in the 1950s, was formalised by I. J. Good as an "intelligence explosion" in 1965, named and popularised by Vernor Vinge in 1993, and made famous by Ray Kurzweil, who predicts human-level AI by 2029 and the singularity by 2045. Critics argue progress follows S-curves, faces physical limits on compute and energy, and depends on slow real-world experiments. Short answer

The technological singularity is the hypothetical moment when artificial intelligence becomes capable of improving itself faster than humans can follow, triggering runaway technological change that makes the future impossible to predict. The idea traces back to John von Neumann in the 1950s, was formalised by I. J. Good as an "intelligence explosion" in 1965, named and popularised by Vernor Vinge in 1993, and made famous by Ray Kurzweil, who predicts human-level AI by 2029 and the singularity by 2045. Critics argue progress follows S-curves, faces physical limits on compute and energy, and depends on slow real-world experiments. Whether it happens or not, the concept shapes how governments, AI labs and researchers think about superintelligence.

The definition in one paragraph

A "singularity" in physics is a point where the usual equations stop working, such as the centre of a black hole. By analogy, the technological singularity is a point beyond which our models of the future break down, because a smarter-than-human intelligence would be shaping events in ways we cannot anticipate. Most versions of the idea share three ingredients:

1. Machines reach human-level general intelligence (AGI). See What is AGI? 2. They improve their own design, producing still smarter machines. 3. The feedback loop accelerates, quickly leading to intelligence far beyond human level. See the intelligence explosion.

How a singularity could actually happen

1. Automated AI research

The most discussed pathway today. If AI systems can write code, run experiments, read papers and propose improvements, AI research itself becomes automatable. Each improvement makes the next one faster. This is the mechanism behind most modern takeoff scenarios. See how to achieve superintelligence.

2. Scaling compute

Training compute for frontier AI has grown several-fold per year for over a decade, driven by GPUs and tensor cores optimised for matrix maths. Bigger models trained on more data have reliably become more capable, as described by scaling laws.

3. Algorithmic efficiency

Better algorithms reduce the compute needed for a given capability. Researchers estimate algorithmic progress has cut compute requirements substantially every year, compounding with hardware gains.

4. Hardware feedback

AI already helps design chips (for example, AI-assisted chip floorplanning). Faster chips enable better AI, which designs faster chips.

5. Brain emulation and enhancement

Alternative routes include emulating a human brain in software or enhancing human intelligence with technology. Both appear further away than AI-driven routes. See superintelligence and human enhancement.

Fast vs slow takeoff

Most researchers today expect something between the extremes: rapid by historical standards, but constrained by physical bottlenecks.

The strongest criticisms

1. S-curves, not exponentials. Most technologies grow exponentially for a while, then level off. Moore's law has slowed; there is no guarantee AI progress continues forever. 2. Physical limits. Compute needs chips, power and data centers. Building gigawatt-scale facilities takes years. See superintelligence compute requirements and AI energy consumption. 3. Diminishing returns. Each improvement may get harder to find (Robin Hanson and others). Smarter systems may face harder problems. 4. The complexity brake. Paul Allen argued understanding intelligence gets harder the deeper we go. 5. Experiments take time. Science, medicine and engineering require real-world testing. Intelligence alone cannot speed up a clinical trial or crop growth. See AI scientific discovery. 6. Economic evidence. Economists such as Robert Gordon note productivity growth has not accelerated the way singularity theories imply. 7. Vague definitions. Without a measurable threshold, the singularity can always be "20 years away."

The case that it is plausible

  • Capabilities on many benchmarks rose dramatically between 2020 and 2026, including coding, mathematics and scientific reasoning. See AI benchmarks explained.
  • AI systems are increasingly used to write code and assist research inside AI labs.
  • Investment in AI infrastructure has reached hundreds of billions of dollars per year.
  • No known law of physics prevents machine intelligence from exceeding human intelligence; the brain is a proof that general intelligence is possible on about 20 watts. See superintelligence vs the human brain.

Measurable signs to watch

Rather than arguing about a single date, track indicators:

1. Share of AI research done by AI: how much code, experiment design and paper writing in labs is automated. 2. Capability per dollar of compute: rising faster than hardware alone would explain suggests algorithmic acceleration. 3. Time horizon of autonomous tasks: how long AI agents can work independently on complex tasks without human help. See AI agents. 4. Scientific output: discoveries made primarily by AI systems. 5. Economic data: productivity growth and AI's share of GDP. 6. Compute build-out: data center power capacity and GPU shipments. See our GPU price tracker.

Frequently asked questions

When will the technological singularity happen?

Nobody knows. Kurzweil predicts 2045; Vinge predicted 2005–2030; many researchers doubt a sudden singularity will occur at all. Forecasts for AGI moved earlier after 2022, but uncertainty remains very high.

Is the singularity the same as AI taking over?

No. The singularity describes rapid, unpredictable change. Whether that change is good or bad depends on whether advanced AI is aligned with human interests. See What is AI alignment?

Who coined the term technological singularity?

The concept is credited to John von Neumann's remarks in the 1950s. Vernor Vinge popularised the modern term in the 1980s and his 1993 essay.

Can the singularity be stopped?

In principle, development can be slowed by regulation or international agreements; in practice, competition makes this hard. See superintelligence governance and the Superintelligence Statement.

Is the singularity science or science fiction?

It is a hypothesis about the future, not established science. Parts of it, such as AI accelerating AI research, are now being studied empirically.
